Good documentation is naturally hard to write, but I think its importance for Physlib cannot be understated.

So I wanted to ask what can be done on a global scale to help ensure that we have the best documentation possible? One answer is naturally write a guide to writing good documentation, but I was wondering if anyone had other suggestions?

Was looking for an acronym of some sorts which would be good to follow related to documentation. The best I can find comes from communication, but I think applies here also. The 5 C's: 1) Clear, 2) Concise, 3) Complete, 4) Correct and 5) Consistent.

This sounds good, I was also thinking about this since your message and maybe updating the agents.md file might be a good move?

I have noticed in my own AI use and also reviews that the documentation does seem to not be concise when AI generated, it might be worth updating this with some excerpts from the guide we come up with?

I agree, I certainly think this is one place that AI really struggles. It is probably one of the main noticeable differences between human written vs AI written PRs, so I think anything we can do in the Agents.md file to aide this will be beneficial.

One thing that might also be worth putting somewhere is the need for heuristic arguments for certain definitions or theorems. It's often the case that I see structures or definitions made in this physlib, and they don't have the "why" associated with it. The "why": Why have we written this definition like this or proved this theorem like that? We could maybe include this more explicitly in some of the doctrines, with a subsection for heuristics in boldface. (Sorry, on my phone and dictated this. So may read odd.)

Mhm this is a very good point, and more than including it explicitly, I think some examples from physlib that we think are good and why they are good might help alot?

An example that jumps to mind for me when I first came to physlib was the classical harmonic oscillator, might be worth doing somewhat of a case study on this file to illustrate the point, the physics is easy to follow and the importance of documentation can hit hard with such an example.
If you have some more examples let me know, when I find some time I will try and open this as a PR

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Good documentation is naturally hard to write, but I think its importance for Physlib cannot be understated.

So I wanted to ask what can be done on a global scale to help ensure that we have the best documentation possible? One answer is naturally write a guide to writing good documentation, but I was wondering if anyone had other suggestions?

In my experience the code is the "what" and the documentation is the "why." That distinction is why LLMs typically do not generate useful documentation -- when all they have as input is the code (the "what"), restating the "what" isn't useful.

There is a way to extract the "why" by reframing how the LLM is prompted. As I use an LLM to generate code, I have the LLM track design choices (trade-offs that are available) and then explain why one option was picked for implementation over the other. Tracking the design options then enables the LLM to create documentation that addresses "why was this implementation chosen?"

If there's code for which design choices wasn't tracked during development, then the process is a bit harder as decision archeology is required. Going back and figuring out "why was this enacted the way it was?" depends on the order in which decisions were made. The dependence on order of choices makes decision archeology challenging.

To summarize, tracking the design choices and capturing why various options were selected for implementation is needed to create documentation that augments the code (rather than merely restating what the code is doing).

If you have the experience of struggling to read someone else's code, one aspect contributing to that is you aren't aware of the reasoning for their design choices, nor the order in which the author faced those choices. The problem is solvable.

I think this is a very nice summary of what makes good documentation and why asking the why is important. I think this comes to the next question, which is: how can we ensure that the documentation in Physlib does have the why in it? On a similar note, how can we make sure that it is as easy as possible for somebody to contain the why in the documentation?

I agree with @Nathaneal Sajan that we need a collection of good examples which can be pointed to - will have a think of any which spring to mind.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

we need a collection of good examples which can be pointed to - will have a think of any which spring to mind.

Zulip is where many of the design decisions are being made. See, for example, #Physlib > Hilbert space for subsets of Space d and #Physlib > Classical Harmonic Oscillator @ 💬
Capturing those is useful but challenging for the LLM, which is why a lot of human curation is needed.

Also, design decisions get re-decided (i.e., a refactor), and then ensuring the alignment of documentation and code is yet another burden.

An example of the difference between human-oriented documentation and LLM-oriented documentation is the relevance of a developer guide versus AGENTS.md. The AGENTS.md has edicts about style, whereas a developer guide explains the rationale motivating the edicts. The LLM just needs to know the project uses Lean; a human developer might want to know "why Lean?" (because PhysLib extends MathLib) and "why not Rocq or Isabelle?" Similarly, the LLM just needs to be told "proofs of lemmas and theorems should be short (under 50 LOC)," whereas explaining to the human why that constraint is relevant should be in a guide for developers/contributors.
Maybe we should have a ./Policies folder or similar to describe such things on the broader scale
